Growth-rule dependence of the viscoelastic gel-point in percolation networks: continuous programming via nucleation density

R. Brown

[Affiliation TBC]

Abstract

The viscoelastic gel-point of a polymer network is commonly treated as a fixed property of chemistry and concentration. Here we demonstrate, through three-dimensional random walk simulations on site-percolation lattices, that the gel-point is instead controlled by the growth dynamics of the forming network and can be continuously programmed via a single nucleation-density parameter. For random (Bernoulli) percolation networks we find pc′ ≈ 0.683 ≈ 1 − pc, quantitatively identifying the rheological gel-point with the loss of spanning connectivity in the void phase. Replacing random growth with adjacency-templated cluster growth shifts the gel-point to pc′ ≈ 0.886 (Δpc′ = +0.20) and qualitatively alters the transition: the critical region is 3.4× broader and probe particles remain persistently sub-diffusive (α ≈ 0.3–0.4) well above pc′. Interpolating via a nucleation-density parameter κ ∈ [0,1] yields a monotonically tunable gel-point spanning Δpc′ ≈ 0.31. GSER-derived frequency-domain spectra confirm the δ(ω) = 45° Winter–Chambon signature at pc′ for both gelation classes.

1. Introduction ✓ written

The gelation of polymer solutions and colloidal suspensions is characterised by a well-defined gel-point pc′ at which the loss tangent tan δ = G″/G′ becomes frequency-independent and equal to unity (Winter–Chambon criterion). This corresponds to a phase angle δ = 45° and a power-law MSD ⟨r²(t)⟩ ∝ t0.5, measurable by passive microrheology through the Generalised Stokes–Einstein Relation (GSER).

What is rarely asked is whether the gel-point is also a function of how the network forms — the spatial growth dynamics of the cluster itself. Here we use 3D random walk simulations on site-percolation lattices to address this directly, demonstrating that the gel-point is not fixed by density alone but is set by the growth dynamics of the network-forming phase, and is tunable via nucleation density.

Three interconnected results are presented: (1) for Bernoulli percolation, pc′ ≈ 1 − pc ≈ 0.683; (2) adjacency-templated growth shifts pc′ to 0.886 (Δpc′ = +0.20, 3.4× broader transition); (3) nucleation-density parameter κ provides continuous control over pc′ ∈ [0.683, 0.993].

2. Model and Methods ✓ written

2.1 Lattice model

3D simple cubic lattice, L = 500, periodic boundary conditions. Sites are classified occupied (network phase) or unoccupied (void/fluid phase). Lattices generated cumulatively: at each p in the sweep, Nnew sites are added to the existing lattice so that higher-p lattices contain all sites present at lower p as a strict subset.

2.2 Growth rules

Bernoulli (κ = 0): Nnew sites selected uniformly at random — classical site percolation. Adjacency-templated (κ = 1): new sites must be adjacent to at least one existing occupied site; 6N and 26N adjacency rules tested. κ-mixing: Nseeds = ⌊(1−κ)Nnew⌋ random seeds per step; remaining sites filled by adjacency growth from the cluster frontier.

2.3 Random walk simulation

NW = 3000 walkers per condition, LW = 106 steps. Walkers on unoccupied sites; blocked moves incur a dwell time (μWT = 20, σWT = 5 steps). Ensemble-averaged MSD computed online.

2.4 Gel-point extraction

α fitted by log–log linear regression over [LW/100, LW/10] = [104, 105] steps. Gel-point pc′ located by linear interpolation where α = 0.5.

2.5 GSER

MSD converted to G*(ω) via the GSER. Since ⟨r²(t)⟩ ∝ tα, the phase angle δ(ω) = 90α is frequency-independent. Physical parameters: T = 293 K, η = 1.2×10−3 Pa·s, a = 0.243 μm, gel mesh l = 10 nm.

3. Results ✓ written

3.1 Gel-point in random percolation: pc′ ≈ 1 − pc

Both Bernoulli-class variants give indistinguishable α(p) curves: α ≈ 1 (Fickian, sol) for p ≲ 0.60, a sharp monotonic decline through α = 0.5, and rapid arrest above pc′. Linear interpolation gives pc′ = 0.6832 (random percolation) and 0.6834 (density increment) — agreement within Δp = 0.0002. The gel-points bracket the void-percolation threshold 1 − pc = 0.6884, with the offset consistent with finite-size effects at L = 500.

Key result: pc′ ≈ 1 − pc. The rheological gel-point coincides with loss of spanning connectivity in the void sublattice. Transition width σsigmoid = 0.015.

3.2 Growth-rule sensitivity: adjacency-templated gelation

Templated variants (6N, 26N) give: pc′ = 0.8856 (6N) and 0.8861 (26N), a shift Δpc′ = +0.20 relative to the Bernoulli class. The transition is 3.4× broader (σsigmoid = 0.052 vs 0.015). Above pc′, α remains 0.3–0.4 even at p = 0.95 (Δp = 0.064) — persistent sub-diffusion absent in the Bernoulli class.

Key result: Δpc′ = +0.20; 3.4× broader transition; persistent sub-diffusion above pc′. Both 6N and 26N give identical results — the connectivity constraint, not the adjacency rule details, drives the shift.

3.3 Continuous tuning via κ-mixing

pc′(κ) is monotonically increasing across the full parameter range, spanning pc′ ∈ [0.683, 0.993]. Two regimes visible in the log-scale panel: a Bernoulli-like regime (κ ≲ 0.99, seed fraction ≳ 1%) with gradual increase, and an Eden regime (κ ≳ 0.99, seed fraction ≲ 1%) with steep increase toward unity.

Key result: Δpc′ ≈ 0.31 total tunable range. κ = 1 extrapolated to pc′ ≈ 0.993 (α = 0.521 at p = 0.99). Regime crossover at ~1% seed fraction.

3.4 Frequency-domain characterisation via GSER

Since ⟨r²(t)⟩ ∝ tα, G′, G″ ∝ ωα and δ(ω) = 90α is frequency-independent (flat horizontal lines in frequency-domain plots). At pc′, both classes exhibit δ ≈ 45° and G′(ω) ≈ G″(ω) — the Winter–Chambon criterion. Panel (c) aligns both classes at Δp = 0 and shows the 4× broader transition directly: the Bernoulli class reaches δ = 22.5° at Δp = 0.016; the Templated class only at Δp = 0.065.

Key result: 4× broader transition directly visible in δ vs Δp. At Δp = 0.064, Bernoulli is nearly arrested (δ ≈ 1°) while Templated retains δ ≈ 23° — persistent sub-diffusion in the frequency domain.

4. Discussion ✓ written

4.1 Physical basis of pc′ ≈ 1 − pc

The result pc′ ≈ 1 − pc is not a numerical coincidence — it is a direct consequence of placing walkers in the void phase. The void sublattice undergoes its own site-percolation transition at 1 − pc. The small offset (0.683 vs 0.6884) is attributable to finite-size effects consistent with L−1/ν scaling with ν ≈ 0.88.

4.2 Why templated growth shifts the gel-point

A compact connected cluster leaves a larger and more interconnected void region than the same number of randomly placed sites — the void loses percolation connectivity only at higher p. Persistent sub-diffusion above pc′ confirms that void channels remain locally open even when disconnected at large scales.

4.3 κ as a material design parameter

κ maps directly onto the number of independent nucleation centres per unit increase in network density — experimentally analogous to cross-linker concentration, temperature ramp rate, or ionic strength in thermoreversible gels.

4.4 Relation to Eden and DLA models

At κ = 1 the model is equivalent to Eden growth. The predicted pc′ → 1 as L → ∞ for κ = 1 is consistent with Eden clusters being compact (fractal dimension → 3), allowing the void to persist to very high density.

4.5 Limitations and future work

Single lattice size (L = 500); finite-size scaling over a range of L needed to extract critical exponents and confirm universality class distinction. κ = 1 gel-point is extrapolated. Future: FSS analysis, 2D and off-lattice systems, connection to experimentally controllable nucleation parameters.

5. Conclusions ✓ written

Three main results are established. First, for Bernoulli percolation networks, the Winter–Chambon gel criterion is satisfied at pc′ ≈ 1 − pc ≈ 0.683, quantitatively identifying the rheological gel-point with loss of spanning connectivity in the void phase. Second, adjacency-templated growth shifts the gel-point by Δpc′ = +0.20 to pc′ ≈ 0.886, with a 3.4× broader transition and persistent sub-diffusion above the gel-point. Third, the nucleation-density parameter κ provides continuous, monotonic control over pc′ ∈ [0.683, 0.993], spanning Δpc′ ≈ 0.31.

GSER-derived frequency-domain spectra confirm the δ(ω) = 45° Winter–Chambon signature at pc′ for both gelation classes, establishing a direct bridge from simulation to measurable microrheology.

These results provide a conceptual and quantitative framework for programming viscoelastic gel-points in network-forming materials through control of cluster growth dynamics rather than chemical composition alone.
